issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The profile is not coherent with a toxic chemical exposure trauma. The selected Threat items are dominated by interpersonal/being-followed danger themes ('someone is following me', lock checking) rather than contamination, health deterioration, environmental exposure, or bodily harm themes that would fit chemical exposure.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: The Maladaptive Strategy item 'Never Alone' is also strongly interpersonal/assault-focused and is hard to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure. 'Avoid Conflict' similarly targets confrontation rather than exposure-related danger, and is not plausibly linked to the selected Threat items or trauma type.

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'Never Alone with another person' is hard to reconcile clinically: it implies fear of interpersonal danger rather than contamination, bodily harm, or environmental exposure. No Trigger, Memory, or Appraisal items support an interpersonal-assault formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Conflict' also points to interpersonal threat management rather than consequences of chemical exposure. With no corroborating interpersonal threat, appraisal, or memory content, this strategy appears misaligned with the trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, avoiding conflict is not a plausible trauma-linked maladaptive strategy unless supported by appraisals about blame, authority, or interpersonal danger, which are absent here. It appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone is hard to reconcile with the stated threat pattern. The threat items emphasize generalized unsafety and checking the physical environment, but not collapse, contamination, or medical emergency fears that would make solitude specifically dangerous after chemical exposure.

vignette:
Dara, a 52-year-old HVAC technician, came for help after a toxic chemical exposure at work that had left him feeling permanently changed. He had been servicing an older commercial cooling unit in a closed mechanical room when a leak released a strong chemical vapor. Within minutes his throat burned, his chest tightened, and he became lightheaded enough that he had to be pulled out by a coworker. Even after the incident ended, the memory of standing in that sealed room, breathing air that suddenly did not feel safe, stayed vivid for him. Since then, he has found it impossible to trust safety even when others reassure him that he is fine. His wife can tell him repeatedly that the house is secure, the doctor can tell him his tests look acceptable, and coworkers can joke that he is overdoing it, but Dara still feels as if danger is hidden just beyond what he can see. He describes his body as constantly tense and ready to react, as though it is braced for another sudden exposure, another invisible mistake in the air.

In the weeks after the event, Dara began living as if any moment of ease could make him vulnerable. He had come to believe that relaxing was dangerous, because the one time he had felt ordinary and focused on the job was the moment the chemical leak caught him off guard. If he sat down after work, let his shoulders drop, or tried to watch television without scanning the room, his mind went immediately back to the sealed mechanical room and the feeling that he had not noticed the threat soon enough. So he stayed busy, pacing the house, doing small repairs, cleaning tools that were already clean, and avoiding anything that could become stressful because stress seemed to sharpen the sense that something was about to go wrong. At home he preferred not to be alone in a room or building; if his wife stepped out to run errands, he often followed her around the house or stood near the front window until she returned. Being by himself in the basement or garage was especially hard, because the silence made him feel trapped with his own body and thoughts.

As time passed, those fears began to shape nearly every part of his day. At night Dara walked through the house checking doors and windows again and again, touching the locks with the same tight concentration each time, unable to settle until he had looked more than once. Even then, the relief never lasted long. He would lie in bed with his muscles rigid, listening for sounds from outside and waiting for the next sign that something was wrong. Because being at ease felt so unsafe, he stopped resting properly after work and avoided the quiet moments that used to help him recover from a long day on the job. On difficult days he called in sick or took longer routes home to avoid anything that might add stress, and the narrowing of his routine began to spill into his marriage. His wife noticed that he no longer sat with her in the evening unless he was also checking the house, and their conversations often became strained when she tried to reassure him. The more she told him he was safe, the less he could believe it; he experienced her reassurance as kind but detached from the reality his body was living in. His vigilance had become its own daily requirement, and the more he watched for danger, the more convincing danger seemed.

Dara's work has also become harder to manage. As an HVAC technician, he still enters buildings, service rooms, and basements, but he now does so with a tightness in his chest and a constant awareness of exits, ventilation, and what might be in the air. He has begun avoiding tasks that feel especially stressful, and when a job requires him to work alone in an enclosed space, he feels a surge of dread that can linger long after he leaves. What once was an ordinary part of his trade now feels like repeated exposure to the very conditions that frightened him most. He has finally sought treatment because the pattern is wearing him down and his wife is worried about how little he sleeps and how rarely he seems able to relax. Dara is not only afraid of another chemical exposure; he is afraid that if he lets his guard down for even a moment, he will miss the next warning sign. What he wants most is to feel safe enough to sit still in his own home, trust a locked door without checking it repeatedly, and be able to do his work without living as though danger is always one breath away.
